text:
Qwen 3.8 Flash Next: drastically faster and much more precise in reaching the result.

Some time ago in this same place someone had suggested having your model create paintings through python (with programming) leaving it quite free. Doing so I had noticed how the model, after creating the first draft, made visual checks and quickly decided what he didn't like, adding corrections just as quickly, he didn't get lost in long, long thoughts... so from this situation I created an additive prompt. in practice I induce the model not to think long thoughts, but just like we hummans do, to jot down a draft, which we gradually improve step by step. I made him do some projects, and t**he model becomes fast, rapid and precise as never before, and above all more self-confident**. Unlike his usual approach, where he tries to map out a plan dozens and dozens of times, fearing he might make a mistake or forget something,  **he ends up wasting a lot of time stuck in pointless loops.**

Here is the prompt I created to add as an addendum to your prompts.

add to your prompt:  
`The construction procedure must be fractal, that is to say you make a rough and basic draft, test it, add details and depth, then test again and add even more details and depth, you have to proceed like this, so you have to start from a very basic and rough draft made from a very rough and basic reasoning, the aim is to start immediately in the creation, observe and decide what to detail. Continue this loop until you consider the work a masterpiece,rich in the kind of detail one would expect from a great artist.`

`EDIT:`

Since I've noticed that when it starts thinking a lot about what to add in the deeper steps, (the pressure of being a great artist makes him less confident again, perhaps it should be removed.) I'm trying to get the model to focus on refining small portions at a time. Here's a modified version; if you have any better suggestions, please let me know.

`The construction procedure must be fractal, that is to say you make a rough and basic draft, test it, add details and depth, then test again and add even more details and depth, you have to proceed like this, so you have to start from a very basic and rough draft made from a very rough and basic reasoning, the aim is to start immediately in the creation, observe and decide what to detail. Continue this loop many times, focus on individual portions of the project until you` `feel they are satisfactory, then move on to the other portions that are rougher until you consider the total work a masterpiece, rich in the kind of detail one would expect from a great artist.`

Try it yourself and tell me your opinion. Perhaps, taken together, we could generalize this procedure better.

China proposes export controls on 23 AI technologies (including large models, agents & clusters); already open-sourced tech is exempted

On October 16, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce and Ministry of Science and Technology released a draft revision to the Catalog of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export. It proposes adding 40 technologies across AI, biomedicine, and solar PV, of which 23 are AI-related (covering foundation/large models, intelligent agents, computing clusters, and information processing technologies).

Public comments are open until November 15. Temporary pre-export registration requirements for the covered technologies take effect immediately.

Key points relevant to open-weight models:

•  Technologies already made public via open-source releases or academic publications are explicitly exempted and not subject to the controls.  
•  Open-sourcing AI technologies, plus certain other activities (e.g., Chinese firms building their own overseas compute centers), are eligible for streamlined automatic licensing.  
•  Providing access via APIs, apps, websites, or SaaS is generally not treated as a technology export.  
•  Overseas local deployment of restricted models can fall under the rules (with possible facilitation in lower-risk cases such as a company’s own overseas cloud).

This is not a blanket ban on open-weight models. However, new models that have not yet been released may face registration or approval steps before their weights or source code can be transferred abroad (thresholds based on performance, parameters, data sensitivity, etc. are still being defined). Chinese labs such as DeepSeek and Qwen could see additional compliance requirements on future open releases.

Source

text:
Agens Volundr 32B v1: we fixed what you flagged in the Preview. 0/50 loops, session continuation, and an MIT engine that runs it with 262K context (measured to 239K) within a 16 GB budget

https://reddit.com/link/1x8yc8d/video/hosf7c1n27wh1/player

Hi r/LocalLLaMA. I'm on the team at Blockway (disclosure: this is our model). Two weeks ago we posted the Volundr 32B Preview here, and you were blunt about what was wrong with it. This is v1, and most of the work went into what you flagged.

WHAT v1 FIXES FROM THE PREVIEW

* "It loops." Repetition loops on SWE-bench tasks: 36/50 → 0/50.
* "It thinks forever." Reasoning steps used to get cut at 32K. Now the median step is 120 tokens and the longest is 12K.
* "No prefix caching, it re-reads the whole history every turn."
   * SGLang build: v1 adds session continuation, so follow-up turns reuse the model's state instead of re-prefilling. Follow-up turns are 2.9× faster on our agent replay (1.6 s median with the drafter), with greedy-equivalent outputs (not byte-identical: a cached prefix is prefilled in different pieces).
   * GGUF: uses llama-server's stock `--ctx-checkpoints` prompt cache, with no custom server code. Our fork only adds the model architecture.
* Agent results: SWE-bench Verified (50-task subset) 22 → 27/50, τ²-bench 89 → 92/120, median SWE task time 124 → 82 min.

"MAKE IT RUN ON CONSUMER GPUS" → AGENS ENGINE (MIT)

We're open-sourcing Agens Engine under the MIT licence. It's an inference engine built for this hybrid architecture: 54 of 72 layers keep a fixed-size state instead of a KV cache, and the engine is designed around that.

* Same GPU, same v1 INT4 weights and drafter, single stream: Agens Engine decodes 1.4–1.6× faster than our own SGLang build (up to 1.8× on code with thinking). Chat 58 → 86, code 79 → 113, agent at 8K context 91 → 121, JSON 125 → 199 tok/s. This is one run per side and compares against our SGLang build only, not stock SGLang, vLLM or llama.cpp, and it is single-stream only.
* New build: Agens-Volundr-32B-v1-Engine-16GB. It's about 2.85 bits/weight (mixed 2/3/4-bit), gives 262K context (we measured up to 239K) within a 16 GB memory budget, and runs only on Agens Engine. A 12 GB build is on the roadmap.
* Honest caveats:
* Speed within the 16 GB budget, single conversation, v1 drafter on:
   * short context: 90 (chat) / 118 (code) / 107 (thinking) / 112 (tool) / 139 (agent, 8K) tok/s
   * after a 219K-token document: 62 / 86 / 77 / 69 / 75 tok/s; 151 s to first token for the 219K prompt
   * a conversation ran to 239K tokens inside the budget
   * weights download is 25 GB
   * These were measured on a 48 GB card under the engine's hard 16 GiB cap (peak 15.5 GiB), not on a real 16 GB card. On a GPU that also drives a display, use a shorter context. Real cards, especially laptop GPUs, may be slower. Post your numbers and we'll add them.
   * At this bit-width, quality drops. GPQA is 73.7 vs 80.3 at bf16 (best of 4 runs each). Coding holds up: HumanEval is 73.2% (1 run) vs 73.8% for INT4. Top-1 agreement with bf16 is 90.4%, KL 0.117. This build is for running locally, not for leaderboard scores.
* Needs Linux, an NVIDIA driver with CUDA 12.9, the NVIDIA container toolkit, and 32 GB+ host RAM for 262K.docker run --gpus device=0 --ipc=host -p 30000:30000
* \-v /path/to/Agens-Volundr-32B-v1-Engine-16GB:/model:ro
* \-v /path/to/Agens-Volundr-32B-v1-DFlash2:/drafter:ro
* ghcr.io/blockwayz/agens-engine:1.0.0 --profile 16gb --model /model --drafter /drafter

STRENGTHS (same harness and settings as our comparison model)

* Competitive coding: LiveCodeBench v6 67.9 (best of 2 runs), +8.4 over Qwen3.8-27B
* Competition maths: AIME 2025 80.0 (best of 2 runs), +6.7 over Qwen3.8-27B
* Long context stays cheap: only 18 of 72 layers keep a KV cache. INT4 (24.6 GB) runs on one 48 GB GPU with a single 131K-token input; 262K configured window (validated to 107K). Decode speed stays flat from 1K to 128K.
* DFlash2 drafter, ships today:
   * JSON / structured output up to 3.0× (125 tok/s INT4 on one 48 GB GPU; 76 tok/s bf16 on a pair)
   * Code 1.9–2.2×
   * Thinking 1.3–1.5×

FULL TABLE (Preview → v1; dips included. Where we ran a benchmark more than once, we report the best of N runs. Every run is listed in the model card footnote.)

|Benchmark|Preview|v1|
|:-|:-|:-|
|SWE-bench Verified (50)|22/50|27/50|
|τ²-bench|89/120|92/120|
|LiveCodeBench v6|63.4|67.9|
|AIME 2025|76.7|80.0|
|MMLU-Pro|79.9|80.0|
|MATH-500|98.2|96.8|
|HumanEval|81.7|78.7|
|GPQA Diamond|84.3|80.3|
|CMMLU|86.5|85.9|
|IFEval|87.6|87.2|
|IFBench|66.3|64.3|
|NIAH (to 107K)|100%|100%|

A few scores went down (GPQA, HumanEval, IFBench). The HumanEval and IFBench dips are within one standard error of the runs; GPQA's isn't. That's the trade-off from tuning for agent behaviour and shorter reasoning. Harness settings are in the footnote under the results table: huggingface.co/Blockway/Agens-Volundr-32B-v1#results-same-harness-for-every-row

Thanks to mmssix on Hugging Face for the independent benchmark write-up in our HF discussions. A lot of the above started there.

KNOWN LIMITATIONS

* 32B, not a frontier model, and we don't claim it is.
* SGLang and llama.cpp still need our builds. Next we're working to upstream the architecture into llama.cpp mainline, and we'll post here when the first PR is open. Stock vLLM can't load it.
* No Metal/Mac in the llama.cpp path yet.
* Agens Engine 1.0 is text only.
